desc: The National Intelligence Program is the intelligence budget that the Director of National Intelligence controls, as distinct from the Military Intelligence Program which the Secretary of Defense controls. Its aggregate appropriated total has been published annually since FY2007 under section 601 of the Implementing Recommendations of the 9/11 Commission Act of 2007 (Public Law 110-53), which requires the DNI to disclose the aggregate amount appropriated within thirty days of the end of each fiscal year; since February 2011 the aggregate request has also been published, under section 364 of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2010. Those are the only two numbers Congress has required to be made public. The appropriated toplines run from $43.5 billion in FY2007 to $73.3 billion in FY2025, with an FY2026 request of $81.9 billion. What is not published is any breakdown whatsoever: not by agency, not by programme, not by intelligence discipline, not by appropriation account. The NIP is not itself an appropriation - it is a cross-cutting programme construct whose money is appropriated inside other bills and other departments' accounts, chiefly the Department of Defense, which is the structural fact that makes the intelligence budget a concealment mechanism rather than merely a secret. A dollar appropriated in a Department of Defense account, scored to the NIP, controlled by the DNI, and executed by a contractor is a dollar with four different institutional owners and one public number.

dossier.denialPosture: The NIP disclosure is a denial wrapped around a concession. The DNI publishes one number and states in the same release that no other currently classified NIP budget information will be disclosed; the Department of War publishes its own number and states that no other MIP budget figures or programme details will be released because they remain classified. Both statements are dated and attributable, and both certify that the composition of the amounts disclosed is placed permanently outside public accounting.
dossier.narrative:
The NIP topline exists as a public number because Congress made it one. Section 601 of the Implementing the Recommendations of the 9/11 Commission Act of 2007, Public Law 110-53, codified at 50 U.S.C. 3306, requires the DNI to disclose the aggregate amount of appropriations requested for, and appropriated to, the National Intelligence Program. Before that statute the topline was itself classified, contested in litigation and estimated by outsiders from budget residue. The 9/11 Commission's reasoning was that a single aggregate number tells an adversary nothing operationally useful while giving the public a minimal handhold on scale. That reasoning is worth holding onto, because it is precisely the reasoning that has never been applied one level down.

The current figures are these. On 21 April 2026 the DNI disclosed an aggregate request of 81.9 billion dollars for the fiscal year 2027 NIP, in ODNI News Release No. 07-26. The same day the Department of War released the MIP topline request for FY2027 at 50.0 billion dollars. Taken together the disclosed US intelligence request for FY2027 is 131.9 billion dollars. The prior year's NIP request, disclosed on 4 June 2025, was also 81.9 billion. For FY2025 the requested figure was 73.4 billion and the appropriated figure, disclosed on 31 October 2025 in ODNI News Release No. 39-25, was 73.3 billion including supplemental funding. The FY2026 to FY2027 step from the low seventies to 81.9 billion is a substantial real increase, and no public account exists of where inside the NIP it went.

What the disclosure statute does not do is the point. The ODNI release states in terms that beyond the topline there will be no other disclosures of currently classified NIP budget information, with the sole exception of unclassified appropriations. The Department of War release mirrors it: the department determined that releasing the top line does not jeopardise any classified activities within the MIP, and no other MIP budget figures or programme details will be released, as they remain classified for national security reasons. Both of those sentences are dated, signed institutional statements, and on this board's method they are catalogued as such. Each is a public certification that the composition of a nine-figure-per-day expenditure is outside public accountability, issued by the same government that says nothing is being concealed about anomalous aerial phenomena.

The structural consequence for the legacy-programme thesis is arithmetic. The NIP and MIP toplines are aggregates over eighteen IC organisations plus the defence services, spanning collection, analysis, counterintelligence, acquisition and personnel. A special access programme, however sensitive, appears in that aggregate as an undifferentiated increment. Move a few hundred million dollars, or a few billion, between elements and the topline moves by a fraction of a percent, well inside the year-to-year variance the public figures already exhibit without explanation. There is no external mechanism that would detect it, because the statute that produces the only public number simultaneously certifies that nothing beneath it will be produced. That is not an allegation about where the money went. It is a statement about what the disclosure regime is capable of showing, which is nothing at the resolution the question requires.

The further complication is that the NIP is not the only channel. Programmes can sit in the MIP rather than the NIP, in service acquisition accounts outside both, in the Department of Energy's weapons complex, or in contractor-held independent research and development recovered through overhead rates on unrelated contracts. A programme domiciled outside the NIP would not appear even as an increment in the one number the public gets. The disclosure regime, in other words, is not a partial window onto the whole. It is a complete window onto one selected pane.

Set against the Brazilian nodes the asymmetry is stark and inverted. Brazil published the substance and never had to publish a price: the Fundo OVNI gives a citizen the report forms, the photographs and the audio, and there is no Brazilian equivalent of an annually disclosed intelligence topline. The United States publishes the price and none of the substance. A citizen of Brazil can read what an air force captain wrote in Para in 1977. A citizen of the United States can learn that 81.9 billion dollars was requested for intelligence in fiscal 2027 and is told, in the same paragraph, that they will learn nothing else. Both governments made a choice about what to make legible. Only one of them chose the part that answers a question.
openQuestions: The FY2026 and FY2025 figures rest on ODNI press-release URLs whose live pages now redirect to the current ODNI newsroom; the figures were confirmed via indexed search results rather than by direct retrieval of the archived release text in this pass.
No public source establishes the internal composition of the NIP at any level below the topline, by agency, by discipline, or by programme, for any fiscal year.

Whether any UAP-related activity is funded within the NIP, within the MIP, within service acquisition accounts outside both, or within Department of Energy accounts is not determinable from any disclosed figure.

The 8.5 billion dollar step from the FY2025 request to the FY2026 and FY2027 requests is unexplained in the public record; whether it reflects inflation, a new mission area, a transfer from MIP, or a programme start is unknown.
The first year in which the NIP topline was disclosed under section 601, and the figure disclosed, have not been verified against a primary ODNI record in this pass.

Contractor independent research and development recovered through overhead on unrelated government contracts is not captured by either the NIP or the MIP topline, and its scale relative to these figures is not established.
dossier.whatItIs: The National Intelligence Program (NIP) is the aggregate budget covering the intelligence activities of the United States Intelligence Community that fall under the Director of National Intelligence's authority, as distinct from the Military Intelligence Program (MIP), which the Department of Defense, since 2025 styled the Department of War, funds and discloses separately. Every year the DNI publicly discloses a single figure: the NIP topline, either the requested appropriation or the enacted one. That single number, and nothing beneath it, is the totality of what the United States tells the public about how much it spends on intelligence.
dossier.whyImplicated: The NIP is the board's measuring instrument rather than a suspect. It is the one intelligence quantity the US government is statutorily obliged to publish, which makes it the only fixed point in an otherwise unmeasurable field, and the disclosure comes bolted to an explicit statement of what will not follow. The DNI's own language is the artefact: beyond the topline figure, there will be no other disclosures of currently classified NIP budget information, the only exceptions being unclassified appropriations. The Department of War's parallel MIP release says the same thing in its own words. So the United States publishes a number in the tens of billions and simultaneously certifies that the composition of that number is not subject to public accounting. For a board premised on a concealed recovery and reverse-engineering effort, this is the structural fact that makes concealment financially unremarkable rather than extraordinary: a programme costing a rounding error against 81.9 billion dollars would not disturb the only figure anyone outside the compartment ever sees. It is also the exact inverse of the Brazilian nodes, where the state published the contents and never had to publish a price.
